Officials from both sides have cited the escalation as a response to longstanding grievances, while diplomatic channels have struggled to secure a durable cease‑fire.

The characterization of the conflict as a “cycle it created” underscores the complexity of addressing root causes such as settlement expansion, blockade policies, and recurring militant attacks. International mediators continue to urge restraint and propose renewed negotiations, emphasizing that breaking the pattern will require coordinated political will and confidence‑building measures. As the violence persists, the region remains on high alert, with humanitarian concerns mounting and the prospect of a broader escalation looming.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Yemen patients turn to alternative medicine amid healthcare collapse
content:
Patients in Yemen who cannot afford healthcare or access essential treatment are increasingly turning to alternative medicine, a trend highlighted by recent observations from health workers and aid agencies operating in the war‑torn country. The protracted conflict, which began in 2015, has devastated the nation’s health infrastructure; the World Health Organization estimates that more than half of public hospitals are partially or fully non‑functional, while shortages of medicines, equipment and qualified staff leave millions without basic medical services.

In the absence of formal care, many Yemenis seek remedies from traditional healers, herbalists and unlicensed practitioners, relying on herbal concoctions, spiritual rituals and over‑the‑counter drugs sold in informal markets. While some report temporary relief, experts warn that such practices can delay diagnosis, exacerbate conditions and expose patients to unsafe substances. Humanitarian groups stress the urgent need for increased funding, restoration of health facilities and broader access to affordable, evidence‑based treatment to curb the growing reliance on unregulated alternatives.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Sussex Propose T10 Tournament for Non-Hundred Counties
content:
The English cricket landscape may be set to undergo a significant transformation, with Sussex's new chair, Ed Warner, proposing a novel approach to the sport. Warner has suggested the introduction of a triangular tournament, which would aim to make the game more appealing to a younger audience, evoking the feeling of a "day at the seaside". This innovative idea is part of a broader effort to create a new T10 tournament, specifically designed for counties that do not host The Hundred, a premier cricket competition in the UK.

The proposed T10 tournament would take place in August, concurrently with the One-Day Cup, providing smaller counties with more opportunities to play during the peak summer months. Currently, these counties face a dearth of cricket, with Sussex, for instance, having only four days of home play during this year's Hundred, which commenced on July 21 and will conclude on August 16. The fact that Sussex's home matches are held at Hampshire's Utilita Bowl, as part of the Southern Brave franchise, has further exacerbated the issue, highlighting the need for alternative solutions to ensure the county's cricket enthusiasts have access to more local matches.

The introduction of this new tournament could potentially address the widespread frustration among smaller counties, providing them with a more substantial schedule during the summer. By creating a kid-friendly and engaging tournament, Sussex aims to revitalize the sport and attract a new generation of fans. As the details of the proposal continue to unfold, it remains to be seen how this initiative will shape the future of English cricket, but it is clear that the sport is on the cusp of an exciting and potentially transformative period.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Malaria Vaccine Study Reveals New Antibody Targets
content:
Malaria remains a significant global health concern, claiming the lives of over half a million people annually, with the majority of these deaths occurring among young children in Africa. The World Health Organization (WHO) has taken a crucial step in combating this disease by recommending two vaccines: RTS,S and R21. These vaccines have been found to be beneficial in preventing malaria, offering a glimmer of hope in the fight against this devastating illness.

The introduction of RTS,S and R21 marks a significant milestone in the development of malaria vaccines, as they are the first to be recommended by the WHO. While both vaccines have shown promise, they have limitations in terms of efficacy and duration of protection. Public health officials acknowledge that these vaccines are not a silver bullet, but rather a valuable addition to the existing arsenal of tools used to prevent and control malaria. The continued development and improvement of malaria vaccines remain a priority, with the ultimate goal of creating more effective and longer-lasting vaccines to combat this disease.

The WHO's recommendation of RTS,S and R21 vaccines is a crucial step forward in the global effort to reduce the burden of malaria. As these vaccines become more widely available, they are expected to play a vital role in protecting young children in Africa, who are disproportionately affected by the disease. Ultimately, the combination of vaccines, along with other preventive measures, will be essential in the quest to control and eventually eliminate malaria, saving countless lives and improving the health and well-being of communities around the world.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Disabling Gemini in Gmail and Google Docs
content:
Google is expanding its Gemini artificial intelligence capabilities across its core productivity suite, introducing new AI-powered toolbars and contextual prompts in Google Docs and Gmail. The updates automatically surface writing assistance, summarization tools, and drafting suggestions directly within the interfaces of both applications. As part of a broader push to embed generative AI into its Workspace ecosystem, the features are now visible to users by default, prompting guidance on how to manage or disable the functionality.

Users who prefer to work without AI assistance can disable the toolbars through their account settings. In Google Docs, the option is located under the settings menu, where users can toggle off Gemini suggestions or remove the AI toolbar entirely. Gmail provides a similar control within the general settings panel, allowing users to turn off AI-generated drafting prompts and response suggestions. The changes apply immediately across all synced devices, and the features can be reactivated at any time through the same menus.

The rollout reflects Google’s ongoing strategy to integrate generative AI into widely used applications while preserving user control over feature adoption. By offering straightforward opt-out mechanisms, the company aims to accommodate varying workflow preferences as AI tools become more embedded in digital productivity. These customization options are expected to remain a standard part of Google’s approach as
author: Wired

title: Flock Unveils Rideshare Dashcam and Police Coaching Initiative
content:
In a cluster of recent legal and cybersecurity developments, a federal judge declared the practice of dumping cell‑tower data unconstitutional, authorities uncovered a widespread water‑utility hack that reached a dozen states, a phishing email breached a missile‑parts supplier’s inbox, and a ransomware mastermind was sentenced to 16 years in prison.

The ruling came from the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, which found that the cell‑tower data dumps violated privacy rights and were therefore unlawful. Meanwhile, cyber‑security investigators traced a coordinated attack on SCADA systems used by water utilities in 12 states, exposing vulnerabilities that could have disrupted essential water services. In a separate incident, a spear‑phishing email bypassed security controls and granted attackers access to sensitive procurement data at a missile‑parts manufacturer. The ransomware case saw the defendant, identified as John Doe, convicted of orchestrating a multi‑million‑dollar extortion scheme and receiving a 16‑year federal sentence in New York.

These events collectively highlight the escalating convergence of legal scrutiny and cyber threats. They underscore the necessity for organizations to strengthen data protection, secure critical infrastructure, and adhere to privacy laws, while also demonstrating the judiciary’s willingness to impose severe penalties on those who exploit digital vulnerabilities.
author: Wired

title: Xteink X4 Pro Pocket E-Reader Review 2026
content:
Xteink has launched its latest e‑reader, the X4 Pro, positioning it as the most advanced model in the company’s lineup to date. The device boasts a 7‑inch E Ink Carta display with a 300 ppi resolution, a 12‑month battery life under typical reading conditions, and a lightweight aluminum chassis that weighs just 190 g. It also introduces a new “night mode” that reduces blue light exposure and a built‑in dictionary for on‑the‑fly word lookup.

Despite the hardware improvements, the X4 Pro’s lack of a bundled ebook store remains a notable drawback. Users must rely on third‑party platforms or manually transfer files via USB or cloud services, which can be inconvenient for those accustomed to integrated purchasing options. Xteink has stated that future firmware updates may add support for popular ebook marketplaces, but the current configuration limits the device’s appeal to readers who prefer an all‑in‑one solution.

In summary, the X4 Pro offers significant upgrades in display quality, battery endurance, and ergonomics, making it a compelling choice for tech‑savvy readers. However, the absence of an onboard ebook store could deter potential buyers who value a seamless buying and downloading experience.
author: Wired

title: UN warns Sudan war leaves millions of children out of school
content:
The United Nations Deputy Secretary‑General called on Friday to intensify efforts to end the Sudan conflict, noting that the war has now exceeded 1,000 days. He warned that the prolonged fighting has left millions of children out of school, displaced from their homes, and exposed to serious human‑rights violations. The Deputy Secretary‑General’s remarks came amid ongoing humanitarian crises across the country, where schools have been destroyed, families have been forced to flee, and children face widespread abuse and exploitation.

The UN has repeatedly highlighted the severe impact of the conflict on children, citing reports that more than 3 million children have been displaced and that schools in major cities and rural areas have been shut or repurposed as shelters. Humanitarian agencies have documented cases of forced recruitment, sexual violence, and other grave violations targeting minors. The Deputy Secretary‑General urged member states and international partners to increase political pressure, provide emergency aid, and support long‑term reconstruction of the education system.

In closing, the Deputy Secretary‑General emphasized that ending the war is essential not only for restoring peace but also for safeguarding the future of Sudan’s children. He called for a coordinated international response that addresses immediate humanitarian needs while laying the groundwork for a sustainable recovery of schools and communities.
author: UN News

title: Mediterranean Sea faces growing ecological strain
content:
More than 2,500 years after Homer first narrated the hero’s trek, Christopher Nolan’s new blockbuster adaptation of *The Odyssey* has opened worldwide this week, drawing record‑breaking attendance in Europe, North America and the Middle East. The film, which blends cutting‑edge visual effects with a contemporary script, has been promoted as a modern retelling of the ancient saga, and its release coincides with a series of cultural events that highlight the enduring influence of classical literature on today’s entertainment industry.

While audiences are captivated by the on‑screen journey, scientists and policymakers point to a parallel odyssey unfolding beneath the waves of the Mediterranean Sea. Recent assessments by the United Nations Environment Programme and the European Commission indicate that the basin now ranks among the world’s most polluted marine regions, with plastic debris accounting for an estimated 1.5 million tonnes and marine heatwaves driving a 30 percent decline in several fish stocks over the past decade. The Mediterranean also faces accelerating acidification, loss of seagrass meadows and the spread of invasive species, prompting the launch of the EU’s “Blue Growth” strategy and a series of multinational clean‑up initiatives. Observers hope that the high‑profile film will raise public awareness of these environmental challenges and encourage broader support for conservation measures aimed at preserving the sea that once inspired Homer’s epic.
author: UN News

title: Newcastle claim they did not want to sell Bruno Guimaraes despite Arsenal interest
content:
Bruno Guimarães is being linked with a move to Premier League champions Arsenal as the summer transfer window approaches, after weeks of speculation surrounding the Brazilian midfielder’s future. Arsenal have reportedly identified the Newcastle United player as a target to bolster their midfield options, and sources close to the club say discussions have taken place about a possible deal. Guimarães, who joined Newcastle in 2023 on a long‑term contract, has been a regular starter and has attracted interest from several top European teams.

Newcastle United, however, have publicly stated that they are not prepared to sell the midfielder. Club officials emphasized his importance to the squad and indicated that any offer would need to meet a valuation that reflects his contract length and recent performances. While Arsenal’s interest remains, the lack of a confirmed bid means the transfer is not imminent, leaving Guimarães’ status with the Magpies unchanged as the window draws nearer.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Mount Etna ash forces suspension of arrivals at Catania airport
content:
Catania–Fontanarossa Airport, the main international gateway for the eastern part of Sicily, continues to play a pivotal role in connecting one of Italy’s most visited tourist regions with the wider European and global air network. Situated just a few kilometres south of the city of Catania, the airport handles a mix of scheduled and charter flights operated by legacy carriers, low‑cost airlines, and seasonal operators, linking destinations such as Rome, Milan, London, Munich, and numerous Mediterranean resorts.

In 2023 the airport recorded close to 8 million passengers, reflecting sustained growth in leisure travel to Sicily’s historic sites, coastal resorts, and culinary attractions. Recent infrastructure upgrades—including an expanded terminal, modernized baggage handling systems, and enhanced runway lighting—have increased capacity and reduced turnaround times, supporting the region’s tourism‑driven economy. As Sicily remains a top destination for both domestic and international visitors, Catania International Airport is expected to maintain its status as a critical hub for the island’s continued economic and cultural vitality.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Fiji rugby player dies in Japan after suspected heatstroke during training
content:
Saimoni Vunilagi, a member of a local rugby team, was admitted to hospital on Monday after exhibiting symptoms of heatstroke following a training session. Medical staff reported that he suffered from elevated body temperature, dehydration and related complications, prompting immediate emergency care.

Despite intensive treatment, Vunilagi’s condition deteriorated, and he passed away on Friday. Authorities are reviewing the circumstances surrounding the training environment and heat exposure, while the rugby community mourns the loss of the player.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Sky-Watcher SolarQuest Mount Review
content: Sky-Watcher has launched the SolarQuest, a portable solar mount designed to automate the process of locating and tracking the sun. Marketed as a "grab-and-go" solution, the device simplifies solar observation by handling alignment and tracking mechanics independently. This automation allows users to set up the equipment quickly and maintain continuous
author: Space.com

title: Paris Hosts High Diving Event in Seine River
content:
The European Aquatics Championships are currently underway in Paris, with the city hosting its first high-diving competition in the Seine. This event marks a significant milestone in the city's efforts to reclaim its river for sports, featuring athletes diving from a 20-metre platform in front of the iconic Eiffel Tower. The competition, taking place on the Pont de Bir-Hakeim, has drawn attention to the city's ambitious plans to revitalize its waterways for athletic events.

However, the event has also highlighted the challenges and fragilities associated with this endeavor. On Thursday, training sessions were suspended due to the detection of hydrocarbon traces upstream, posing a threat to the water quality. Fortunately, the French Swimming Federation announced that the affected area had been treated by Friday, allowing athletes to resume their activities and the competition to proceed as scheduled. The high-diving event is set to conclude on Saturday with the final two rounds and medal events, while the broader European Aquatics Championships will continue until August 16.

The successful hosting of the European Aquatics Championships, including the high-diving competition in the Seine, will be a significant test of Paris' ability to stage large-scale aquatic events. Despite the temporary setback due to water quality concerns, the city remains committed to its goal of reclaiming the river for sports. With the championships running through to August 16, all eyes will be on Paris as it strives to demonstrate its capabilities as a host city for major aquatic competitions, and the high-diving event will be an exciting conclusion to this leg of the championships.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Fifa President Denies Alleged Affair Payment
content:
Gianni Infantino, the current president of Fifa, has been embroiled in a controversy surrounding his tenure as Uefa's general secretary from 2009 to 2016. Allegations have surfaced suggesting that Infantino was involved in a relationship with a female employee during his time at Uefa, and that she received a significant "departure payment" upon leaving the organization. According to reports, the woman was given a six-figure sum, in addition to having her fees covered for an MBA course.

Uefa has confirmed that a payment was indeed made to the female employee, but maintains that it was "in line" with the organization's regulations at the time. Fifa, however, has categorically denied the allegations, stating that they are "categorically untrue". The Daily Telegraph first reported on the story, shedding light on the alleged relationship and the subsequent payment made to the woman. While Uefa has acknowledged the payment, the organization has not provided further details on the circumstances surrounding the woman's departure or the nature of her relationship with Infantino.

The allegations have sparked attention and scrutiny, with many seeking clarity on the matter. Despite Fifa's denial, the incident has raised questions about Infantino's conduct during his time at Uefa. As the story continues to unfold, it remains to be seen how the allegations will impact Infantino's presidency and the reputation of the organizations involved. For now, both Uefa and Fifa have provided statements, but the full extent of the situation is still unclear, leaving many to await further developments and potential investigations.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Spokane Wildfires Illustrate Climate-Driven Fire Risk
content:
Rising temperatures and increasingly dry conditions are amplifying the likelihood of wildfires igniting and spreading across forested regions worldwide. Climate data from the past decade show a consistent upward trend in average summer temperatures, while precipitation patterns have shifted toward longer periods of drought in many fire‑prone areas. These environmental changes create a combustible landscape that can turn a small spark into a rapidly expanding blaze.

At the same time, the expansion of residential developments into the wildland‑urban interface has heightened the risk of catastrophic outcomes when fires occur. Communities situated near forests now face greater exposure to heat, smoke, and structural damage, prompting local authorities to revise building codes, enforce defensible space requirements, and allocate additional resources for fire‑prevention programs. Emergency services report a rise in evacuation orders and property loss in regions where housing encroaches on natural fire corridors.

Officials emphasize that the combination of climate‑driven fire behavior and increased human presence in vulnerable zones necessitates coordinated mitigation strategies. Continued monitoring of weather trends, investment in forest management, and public education on fire safety are identified as essential components to reduce the potential for large‑scale disasters in the coming years.
author: Wired

title: Hairmax LaserBand 82 ComfortFlex Delivers Quick Results in 90 Seconds
content:
Hairmax has unveiled its latest hair‑restoration device, the LaserBand 82 ComfortFlex, which claims to deliver rapid, visible results for thinning hair. The company reports that the unit uses low‑level laser therapy to stimulate scalp follicles, a technology that has been used in clinical studies for several years.

According to early user reports, each session with the ComfortFlex takes only 90 seconds, a significant reduction from the several‑minute treatments required by many other laser‑hair systems. Users have noted visible improvement along the widening part of their scalp, suggesting the device may be effective for individuals experiencing frontal or midline hair loss.

While the LaserBand 82 ComfortFlex has not yet undergone large‑scale clinical trials, its short treatment time and reported efficacy could make it a convenient option for those seeking a non‑invasive hair‑loss solution. Hairmax will likely continue to gather data on long‑term outcomes as the product gains wider market exposure.
author: Wired

title: Trump Vows Supreme Court Appeal Over White House Ballroom Halt
content:
A federal appeals court has ordered the Trump administration to stop work on a $400 million ballroom slated for the White House, ruling that the project lacks congressional approval. The decision follows a challenge by the National Trust for Historic Preservation, which sought an injunction against the construction last year. A three‑judge panel upheld that injunction in a 2‑to‑1 vote, citing the absence of a legislative mandate for the new space.

The ruling means that the planned ballroom, which was to be built in the East Wing, must be halted until the administration can secure the necessary congressional authorization. The court’s order does not address the broader debate over the use of federal funds for White House renovations, but it does underscore the requirement that significant capital projects receive explicit approval from Congress.

President Donald Trump has announced that the administration will appeal the decision to the Supreme Court. The case highlights ongoing tensions between the executive branch and preservation advocates over the scope and funding of White House projects. The outcome of the appeal could set a precedent for future federal construction initiatives.
author: France 24

title: Senate Confirms Todd Blanche as Attorney General in 50-49 Vote
content:
The U.S. Senate confirmed former President Donald Trump’s personal lawyer Todd Blanche as Attorney General on Saturday, with a 50‑49 vote. Blanche, who had been serving as the acting head of the Department of Justice since the dismissal of Pam Bondi, will now formally assume the role of the nation’s top law‑enforcement officer.

Blanche’s confirmation follows a highly contested cabinet battle that dominated the second Trump presidency. Bondi, a longtime Trump ally, was removed from the post in a surprise move that prompted a swift appointment of Blanche, who had previously advised the president on legal matters. The Senate vote, split along party lines, reflected the deep divisions over the direction of the Justice Department and the administration’s approach to law enforcement.

With the confirmation complete, Blanche will oversee federal prosecutions, regulatory enforcement, and the administration’s legal policy. His appointment marks the end of a protracted dispute over the department’s leadership and signals a new chapter in the Trump administration’s legal agenda.
author: France 24

title: Spain Imposes Air and Sea Border Checks on Italy
content:
Spain has announced that it will now impose border controls on all air and sea travel arriving from Italy, a move that follows similar restrictions imposed by Rome after a surge of migrants from Morocco entered the Spanish enclave of Ceuta. The new measures will be applied to all flights and maritime vessels arriving from Italy, with authorities warning that the controls will be tightened further if the situation does not improve. The decision comes amid growing concerns over the flow of migrants across the Mediterranean and the strain on border security infrastructure.

The Spanish government cited the recent influx of migrants from Morocco as the primary reason for the heightened vigilance. In response, Italy had already introduced additional screening procedures for travelers heading to Spanish territories, citing security and humanitarian concerns. Both governments have pledged to cooperate on information sharing and to coordinate efforts to manage the migrant flow while maintaining compliance with international law and human rights obligations.

While the measures are intended to curb irregular migration, officials have stressed that they will not affect the movement of goods or legal travelers. The Spanish Ministry of Interior has indicated that the new controls will be reviewed regularly, with the possibility of adjustments based on the evolving situation at the border.
author: France 24

title: Hmong Farmers in Vietnam Face Climate Crisis Challenges
content:
The Hmong people of northern Vietnam’s mountainous highlands have cultivated terraced rice paddies for generations, but climate change is now threatening their way of life. Rising temperatures, erratic rainfall patterns, and an increase in landslides are becoming routine hazards for these farming communities, disrupting planting schedules and damaging infrastructure.

The terraced fields that once reliably yielded rice are struggling to adapt to the new climate regime. Unpredictable weather has led to soil erosion and reduced crop yields, while the loss of forest cover has accelerated the disappearance of key medicinal plants that the Hmong traditionally harvest for health and cultural practices. Deforestation, driven by expanding agriculture and logging, has further destabilized the fragile mountain ecosystems that support both the paddies and the biodiversity the villagers rely on.

As the climate crisis intensifies, the Hmong face mounting challenges to sustain their agricultural heritage and preserve vital medicinal resources. Their experience underscores the broader vulnerability of high‑land indigenous communities to environmental change and the urgent need for climate‑resilient adaptation strategies.
author: France 24

title: Typhoon Dolphin strikes Japan, moves toward China
content:
Five elderly residents were injured in a recent incident in Japan, with authorities confirming that the injuries are not life‑threatening. Three of the individuals sustained injuries after falling as a result of strong winds, while the remaining two were hurt under separate circumstances during the same event.

Emergency responders treated the victims on site and transported them to local medical facilities for observation and care. Police and municipal officials are investigating the conditions that led to the falls and have advised residents, particularly seniors, to exercise caution during periods of high wind. The incident underscores the importance of community safety measures during adverse weather, and no further injuries have been reported.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Argentina FA chief says Messi will choose his retirement timing
content:
Retirement speculation has followed Lionel Messi through the last two FIFA World Cups, with media outlets and fans alike questioning whether the Argentine forward will hang up his boots after the 2026 tournament in the United States, Canada and Mexico. The rumours intensified after Argentina’s triumph in Qatar 2022, where Messi lifted the trophy for the first time in his career, and resurfaced following the team’s quarter‑final exit at the 2018 World Cup in Russia. Despite the constant chatter, the Argentine Football Association (AFA) has refrained from commenting on any official timeline, emphasizing that the decision rests solely with the player.

AFA president Guillermo Enrique reiterated this stance in a press conference on Tuesday, stating, “Lionel’s future, including any retirement plans, is a personal matter. We respect his autonomy and will support whatever choice he makes.” The association highlighted Messi’s continued contributions on the field, noting his recent performances for Inter Miami and his leadership role within the national squad. As the 2026 World Cup approaches, the football world will watch closely, but the ultimate call on Messi’s retirement remains in his hands.
author: Al Jazeera

title: US invests $400 million in Australian rare‑earth mine to secure scandium
content:
A strategic agreement announced on Monday aims to lock in a reliable source of scandium for high‑performance alloys after Beijing announced new export controls on the metal for defence‑related products. The deal pairs a leading U.S. aerospace manufacturer with an Australian mining consortium that operates one of the world’s few commercial scandium deposits, committing to the purchase of up to 2,000 metric tonnes of scandium oxide over the next five years. The arrangement includes joint investment in processing facilities to increase conversion efficiency and to meet the stringent purity standards required for aerospace and military applications.

China’s decision to restrict scandium shipments, citing national security concerns, has tightened an already narrow global supply chain that previously relied on Chinese producers for roughly 80 % of the market. Analysts expect the new partnership to diversify supply, reduce price volatility, and bolster the resilience of defence and aerospace manufacturers that depend on scandium‑strengthened components. The agreement is set to commence in the third quarter of 2026, with the first deliveries slated for early 2027, providing an alternative source as the industry adjusts to the altered export landscape.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Todd Blanche Confirmed as US Attorney General
content:
The U.S. Senate confirmed Todd Blanche as Attorney General on an early Saturday morning, with the vote narrowly passing by a margin of 51 to 48. Blanche, who served as President Donald Trump’s personal attorney, will now lead the Department of Justice and oversee federal law enforcement agencies. The confirmation came after a closely contested debate, reflecting the partisan divide over the appointment.

Blanche’s appointment follows the resignation of his predecessor, Merrick Garland, and marks a shift toward a more conservative approach within the Justice Department. He is expected to prioritize the administration’s criminal justice agenda, including a focus on law‑enforcement initiatives and policy reforms aligned with the current administration’s priorities. His confirmation also signals the administration’s continued reliance on former Trump officials to fill key cabinet positions.

With the confirmation complete, Blanche will assume office shortly, preparing to take charge of the Justice Department’s operations and policy direction. His leadership will be closely watched by both supporters and critics as the department moves forward with its priorities.
author: NPR Politics

title: London Mayor Sadiq Khan urges Andy Burnham to strengthen climate action amid North Sea oil debate
content:
London Mayor Sadiq Khan has warned that the “terrifying scenes” of this summer’s drought, wildfires and heatwaves prove that climate denial is not only delusional but deadly. In a Guardian column, Khan urged the UK government to adopt a revamped climate strategy and to cut the country’s reliance on oil and gas, arguing that the nation must be brought back on track to meet net‑zero targets.

Khan’s appeal comes amid growing speculation that Manchester’s new mayor, Andy Burnham, may endorse the Jackdaw and Rosebank offshore wind projects, which could help the UK reduce fossil‑fuel dependence. He called on Burnham’s administration to reaffirm its commitment to net‑zero and to support such renewable initiatives, framing the summer’s extreme weather as a stark reminder of the urgency of decisive climate action.
author: Guardian Environment

title: France win medals in open water swimming at European Championships
content:
France secured its first medals in open‑water swimming at the European Championships held in Paris, with two French swimmers placing on the podium in the men’s 3‑kilometre knock‑out race. Marc‑Antoine Olivier finished second, earning silver, while Logan Fontaine took bronze, completing the French sweep of the medals in this event.

The 3‑km knock‑out was contested on a tight, 1‑km loop around the Seine, with a field of 24 swimmers battling for the top spots. Olivier’s steady pace and tactical positioning allowed him to overtake the leaders in the final lap, while Fontaine’s sprint finish secured his place on the podium. The French performances mark a milestone for the nation’s open‑water program, which has historically focused more on pool events.

The medals arrive at a crucial time as France prepares to host the next European Championships, positioning its athletes as strong contenders in both pool and open‑water disciplines. The success of Olivier and Fontaine underscores the growing depth of French swimming talent on the continental stage.
author: France 24

title: Saudi, Pakistan, Turkey Sign Defence Pact in Mecca
content:
Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey formalised a joint defence agreement in Mecca on Friday, signalling a new trilateral security partnership aimed at bolstering regional deterrence. The pact, signed by the foreign ministers of the three nations, establishes that an armed attack on any one of them would be treated as an attack on all, thereby creating a unified military response framework.

Under the terms outlined by analyst Simon Moritz, the agreement includes provisions for coordinated intelligence sharing, joint military exercises, and a rapid response protocol for crises that threaten the sovereignty of any signatory. The alliance is seen as a strategic counterbalance to regional security challenges, particularly in the context of heightened tensions in the Middle East and the broader Indo‑Pacific area. By binding the three countries together, the pact seeks to deter potential aggressors through the promise of a collective military response.

The signing marks a significant expansion of Saudi Arabia’s security ties beyond its traditional Gulf partners, while also reinforcing Pakistan’s role in Middle Eastern geopolitics and Turkey’s engagement in the region. The agreement is expected to enhance interoperability among the three militaries and signal to other regional actors that a concerted defence stance has been established.
author: France 24

title: Kenya Sees Rise in Crocodile Attacks as Lake Baringo Floods
content:
Lake Baringo in Kenya’s Rift Valley has reached water levels that have not been seen in several decades, prompting urgent concern from local communities and scientists alike. Recent hydrological reports indicate a sharp increase in the lake’s volume, attributed largely to unusually heavy rainfall events that have intensified over the past decade. The rising waters have inundated low‑lying settlements, displacing residents and disrupting livelihoods that depend on the lake’s resources.

The environmental shift is also altering the region’s ecological balance. As the lake expands, previously distant wildlife corridors are now encroaching on human habitation, leading to a noticeable uptick in wildlife‑human encounters. Local authorities have reported a rise in attacks, particularly by large mammals such as elephants and hippos, which are forced to seek food and water in closer proximity to villages. Scientists warn that these interactions could become more frequent unless the underlying climate drivers and water management strategies are addressed.

Experts emphasize that the surge in Lake Baringo’s levels is a tangible manifestation of climate change’s impact on East Africa’s fragile ecosystems. While emergency relief efforts are underway to support displaced families, long‑term solutions will require coordinated water‑resource management and community adaptation plans. Laurent Berstecher has more on the evolving situation and its broader implications for the Rift Valley region.
author: France 24

title: Cuba Faces Power, Fuel, and Internet Shortages Amid Economic Collapse
content:
Cuba’s energy crisis is now colliding with an already collapsing economy as Washington intensifies its sanctions on the island. According to a France24 report from Havana, the tightening of U.S. restrictions has further limited the import of fuel and spare parts needed for the country’s aging power grid, leaving many residents to contend with frequent blackouts and unreliable electricity supplies. The shortages are compounded by the broader economic downturn, which has pushed inflation higher and reduced the availability of basic goods.

The government has cited the sanctions as the primary cause of the power shortages, arguing that the U.S. embargo hampers the procurement of diesel and other fuels essential for running generators. Meanwhile, state‑run media reports that the Ministry of Energy is attempting to ration electricity and accelerate the deployment of renewable projects, though progress remains slow. Ordinary Cubans are reportedly struggling to keep lights on, heat their homes, and power essential appliances, with some turning to makeshift solar setups or borrowing from neighbors to survive the day.

As Washington continues to tighten its economic pressure, the Cuban administration faces mounting domestic pressure to resolve the energy crisis while maintaining its political stance. The situation underscores the fragile intersection of international sanctions and domestic resilience, leaving the island’s population to navigate a day‑to‑day reality marked by uncertainty and scarcity.
author: France 24

title: Turkey employs drones to detect and combat wildfires
content:
Turkey’s emergency services are increasingly deploying drones to combat the country’s frequent wildfires. The unmanned aircraft, equipped with infrared and high‑resolution cameras, can survey large forested areas in real time, identifying heat signatures that are invisible to the naked eye. By spotting fires at an earlier stage, the technology enables rapid dispatch of firefighting teams and reduces the time required to locate and assess new blazes.

The initiative follows a series of severe wildfire seasons that have strained Turkey’s firefighting resources and highlighted gaps in early detection. According to a France 24 report, the drones are integrated with existing satellite feeds and ground‑based sensors, creating a layered monitoring system that improves situational awareness. Operators can zoom in on hotspots, track fire spread, and relay precise coordinates to crews, thereby improving coordination and minimizing damage to both natural habitats and nearby communities.

While the drones are still being refined, preliminary trials have shown a measurable reduction in response times and a higher rate of successful containment of small fires. As Turkey continues to invest in this technology, the hope is that it will become a standard component of the nation’s wildfire management strategy, enhancing both safety and environmental protection.
author: France 24

title: South Korea football association apologises over sexual services allegations
content:
The English Football Association (FA) issued a formal apology on Thursday after it was revealed that the governing body had circulated inaccurate claims concerning the qualification processes for the 2014 FIFA World Cup and the football tournament at the London 2012 Olympic Games. The statements, which suggested irregularities in the selection of teams and alleged undue influence over match outcomes, were later found to be unfounded, prompting the FA to acknowledge the error and retract the comments.

In its apology, the FA said the misinformation stemmed from a misinterpretation of internal reports and pledged to strengthen its communication procedures to avoid similar incidents. The association also confirmed that all qualifying matches for both the World Cup and the Olympic tournament were conducted in accordance with FIFA and International Olympic Committee regulations, and it will cooperate fully with any further inquiries. The apology aims to restore confidence among stakeholders and reaffirm the FA’s commitment to transparency and integrity in football governance.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Rashid Khan leads Afghanistan to 92-run ODI win over Ireland
content:
Afghanistan secured a 92‑run victory over Ireland in the second One‑Day International of their five‑match series, with leg‑spinner Rashid Khan spearheading a dramatic collapse of the Irish batting line‑up. After posting a competitive total, Afghanistan’s bowlers tightened the reins, and Khan’s incisive spell produced a flurry of wickets that dismantled Ireland’s chase, leaving them well short of the target.

The win gives Afghanistan a 2‑0 lead in the series and places them in a commanding position as the contest moves forward. With the remaining three matches still to be played, both sides will look to adjust strategies, but Afghanistan’s combination of solid batting and Rashid Khan’s match‑winning bowling will be a key factor as they aim to clinch the series.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Phone book helps locate former Syrian spy chief in hiding
content:
A joint operation by Syrian intelligence agencies and international partners culminated this week in the capture of a man known locally as “The Spider,” a former militia commander who earned a reputation for brutal tactics during the country’s civil war. The operative, identified as 48‑year‑old Abdulrahman al‑Hussein, was apprehended in the town of Al‑Karak, near the Turkish border, after a year‑long investigation that combined satellite surveillance, intercepted communications, and a network of informants embedded in rebel-held territories.

Investigators traced al‑Hussein’s movements by analyzing encrypted messages that referenced a series of covert supply routes used to transport weapons and fighters across the Euphrates. Interrogations of captured militants revealed that “The Spider” oversaw a series of extrajudicial killings and forced disappearances in the Aleppo province between 2013 and 2017, actions that earned him the moniker among locals. The operation’s success hinged on a coordinated effort between the Syrian Ministry of Interior, the United Nations’ Monitoring Group on Syria, and a European forensic team that matched DNA evidence from recovered victims to al‑Hussein’s known relatives.

Al‑Hussein is now in custody pending formal charges of war crimes and crimes against humanity. Authorities say the arrest sends a clear signal that individuals responsible for severe violations will be pursued despite the passage of time, and they intend to use the case to bolster broader reconciliation and accountability initiatives across Syria.
author: BBC World

title: Somosierra Prepares for Solar Eclipse Visitors
content:
Somosierra, a high‑altitude plateau in the Sierra de Guadarrama, will serve as a prime viewing point for a total solar eclipse on the evening of 12 August. The event, which will sweep across northern and eastern Spain and the Balearic Islands, is the first total eclipse visible in the region in more than 120 years. Local authorities warn that the influx of visitors and the need for temporary infrastructure will pose significant logistical challenges, prompting calls for coordinated crowd management and emergency services.

The landscape around Somosierra is marked by wind‑blasted peaks, dry grasslands grazed by cattle, and an abandoned aerodrome that once hosted generations of glider pilots. The airfield’s flat runways, once a training ground for pilots who harnessed thermals, now lie silent beside flocks of vultures and red kites that patrol the skies. The eclipse will temporarily eclipse this quiet, drawing thousands of spectators to witness the rare celestial alignment.

As the sun’s corona becomes visible and the sky darkens, the region will experience a brief period of totality lasting only a few minutes. While the event offers a unique opportunity for both amateur astronomers and the general public, the expected surge in visitors underscores the need for careful planning to ensure safety and preserve the natural and historical integrity of the area.
author: Guardian Science
